name: The Dark Side of the Moon

info.label: EMI Records
info.desc: The Dark Side of the Moon is the eighth studio album by English rock band Pink Floyd, released on 1 March 1973 by Harvest Records. The album built on ideas explored in earlier recordings and live shows, but lacks the extended instrumental excursions that characterized their earlier work. Its themes explore conflict, greed, the passage of time, and mental illness, the latter partly inspired by the deteriorating mental state of founding member and principal contributor, Syd Barrett. Developed during live performances, an early version was premiered several months before recording began; the new material was recorded in two sessions in .
info.engineers: Alan Parsons, Peter James / Bernie Grundman, James Guthrie, Joel Plante

podcast.body: Pink Floyd recorded their eighth studio album at Abbey Road Studios in London. It features "The Great Gig in the Sky," a song developed from Richard Wright's chord progression and enriched by Claire Torry's unique vocal performance, becoming one of their most iconic tracks. "In 1973, Pink Floyd was working on their eighth studio album at Abbey Road Studios in London."

podcast.body: The iconic album cover for "The Dark Side of the Moon" was designed by Storm Thorgerson, renowned as one of the most famous album art creators of all time. His work on this cover is considered a seminal piece in album art history. "So yeah, Dark Side of the Moon... all are his creations."

This album recently marked its 43rd anniversary, an event tied to one of its three official releases. Its initial launch was considered a disaster, leading to multiple official release dates, driven by intense anticipation. The record company prematurely released the album before it was fully completed or out of post-production. The most significant official presentation, also commemorating its 43rd anniversary, took place at the London Planetarium, a venue chosen for its thematic alignment with the album's cover and overall concept. Despite the official presentation, the band, upset that the album was unfinished, boycotted the event. Specialized press attending the launch found only life-sized cardboard cutouts of the band members with the album playing, as the band refused to be present for its own release under these circumstances. Upon release, the album quickly reached number one on the charts but only held that position for a single week. Remarkably, it then spent approximately 15 years, or about 800 consecutive weeks, on the Billboard 200 list of best-selling albums in the United States, an extraordinary feat that, while not a record, came very close. It is recognized as one of the best conceptual albums in music history and a defining work in Pink Floyd's career. While the music itself is highly important, the band's primary focus during its creation was on the concept, not just the musical composition. The album integrates compositions, melodies, and even complete songs that pre-existed Pink Floyd's official albums, having been previously used in concerts but not recorded. The band aimed for a solid conceptual album with a very closed narrative, leading them to adopt a clearer and more direct lyrical language and to discard any material that didn't perfectly align with the album's themes. This represented an intensification of an evolutionary process within Pink Floyd, marking it as possibly their first truly great conceptual album and setting a new direction for the band's musical development. The complex development of its conceptual thread, rather than just the music, began almost a year prior; in February 1972, the band previewed a significant portion of the album's melodies and songs in London to specialized press and critics, who were amazed by what they heard but had to wait a full year for the album's release. The album's central concept is "the hardest aspects of the human condition." Two significant thematic influences were the mental deterioration of Syd Barrett, Pink Floyd's original leader, whose delicate emotional health and eventual retreat into reclusion due to severe mental problems (brought on by the band's success and record label pressures) deeply impacted the band's early career and ongoing exploration of madness and psychological evolution. Another important influence was philosophy, which the band began to seriously integrate as a mental thread and theme within their songs, expanding on their existing mystical and philosophical leanings. The album delves into themes such as madness (beyond Syd Barrett's specific case), hatred, greed, fear, consumerism, aggression, depression, and the fear of death, exploring these difficult aspects of human evolution throughout life. The album is divided into two parts, Side A and Side B. Side A approaches the harshness of the human condition from a personal and interior perspective: the first song addresses human madness or the loss of mental control; the second discusses regaining mental control and taking charge of one's life after losing direction; the third speaks of the refuge and reflection found once control is re-established; the fourth explores refuge and solitude after recovery and reflection; and the final song is an allegory of death at the end of life, once control has been regained. Side B examines the same themes but from a social viewpoint, focusing on how society and groups affect the individual. It touches upon greed, racial prejudice, consumerism, and the unhappiness induced by a society devoted to work and suffering. Side B analyzes this societal situation, offering a final conclusion, and again uses allegories, particularly mental illness, as a source of inspiration, but this time focusing on how a hostile environment can drive people to madness. Side B culminates in what the band called "catharsis," leading to a vision of liberation, a more humble understanding of the world, and a collective and cooperative perspective that champions unity for the common good over the societal competition that ultimately leads to madness and unhappiness. The album is musically incredible, considered one of the best in history, but its true significance lies in its profound conceptual nature, offering deep thoughts and a critical vision of society in the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, marking a new, revolutionary way of working for Pink Floyd. "el Darkseller de Moon fue el último álbum que acabaron grabando Pink Floyd con capito de récord, se aparte de la isa que borrón pinta su relación."

podcast.body: This iconic album featured early synthesizer experimentation, particularly on the instrumental track "On the Run." The band was intrigued by the new sonic possibilities offered by synthesizers, using a primitive model without a keyboard, the EMS VCS III. "If you go back to Dark Side of the Moon and the Instrumental Track on the Run, we hear primitive synthesizer, one without a keyboard called an EMS VCS III."

podcast.body: A drum set reportedly used to record Pink Floyd's iconic album "Dark Side of the Moon" was present in John Mayer's old mansion studio in Calabasas, California. Ash Boo Shultz of USS leaned against it while channeling inspiration for the song "Who's With Me." "The guy who who runs the studio walks in and he said he goes oh that's the that's the drum set for that they recorded dark side of the moon on."
